{"id": "132817515ecf43b998516138934ff749", "role": "user", "content": [{"text": "Fast agent report: a separate fast agent investigated this same incident in parallel and has finished. This is its whole final report, shared once. Nobody has checked it.

## Root cause
The limit is the EBS volume, not the instance. Starting about 16:17 UTC, a write-only workload with 8 KiB writes began on io2 volume vol-0123456789abcdef0 (10 GiB, 1,000 provisioned IOPS). Since 16:20 the volume has handled exactly 1,000 write ops per second, every 5-minute period. That matches its provisioned IOPS exactly, so the volume is capped. The extra requests wait in a queue: average queue depth is about 1.33 and each write takes about 1.33 ms, which is the higher write latency your application sees. The VolumeQueueLength \u003e 1 alarm fired at 16:23:04.

Throughput is not the problem: about 8.2 MB/s is far below what this io2 volume allows. The instance is not the problem either. i-1234567890abcdef0_3 is a c6i.xlarge with a baseline of 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s. Its InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck stayed at 0, and its EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99%.

What to change: raise the provisioned IOPS on vol-0123456789abcdef0 with ModifyVolume, for example to 3,000–4,000. At 10 GiB, io2 allows up to 1,000 IOPS per GiB, so 10,000 is the most it can take without growing the volume. The change applies online.

One caveat: the instance's EBS bandwidth is shared. Total EBS throughput on the instance is already about 139 MB/s of its 156.25 MB/s baseline, and almost all of that is gp3 vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 reading about 131 MB/s, which is its own 125 MiB/s cap. At 8 KiB per write, each additional 1,000 IOPS on the io2 adds about 8 MB/s. Going much above about 3,000 IOPS on the io2 while volume b keeps reading at full speed will reach the instance baseline and lean on burst credits. If you need more than that, also move to a larger instance size (for example c6i.2xlarge or bigger), or reduce or reschedule the gp3 read job.
## Evidence
- CloudWatch alarm example-a-io2-queue-length went to ALARM at 2026-11-23 16:23:04 UTC: VolumeQueueLength was about 1.333 for 16:20–16:22, against a threshold of 1.0.
- ec2 describe_volumes: vol-0123456789abcdef0 is io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000, attached to i-1234567890abcdef0_3 as /dev/sdf.
- AWS/EBS VolumeWriteOps (5-minute sums) from 16:20 to 16:40: 299,989–300,015 per period, which is about 1,000 IOPS and equal to the provisioned limit. Read ops were 0. Before 16:15 there was no I/O.
- AWS/EBS VolumeWriteBytes is about 2.4576e9 per 5 minutes: 8,192 bytes per op and about 8.2 MB/s, far below any throughput limit.
- AWS/EBS VolumeTotalWriteTime is about 400 s per 300,000 ops, so about 1.33 ms per write. VolumeQueueLength went from 0 (baseline 15:50–16:10) to about 1.33–1.34 (16:20–16:45).
- AWS/EC2 InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck were 0 for every period from 15:50 to 16:45. EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% stayed at 99%, so the instance was not throttling.
- describe_instance_types c6i.xlarge: EBS baseline is 6,000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s; maximum is 40,000 IOPS and 1,250 MB/s.
- Same instance, vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 (gp3, 3,000 IOPS, 125 MiB/s): about 3.93e10 bytes read per 5 minutes, which is about 131 MB/s and right at its throughput cap (alarm example-b-gp3-read-bytes went to ALARM at 16:23:18). Combined with the io2, the instance uses about 139 of its 156.25 MB/s baseline.
## Affected resources
- vol-0123456789abcdef0 (io2, example-a-io2)
- i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (c6i.xlarge)
- vol-1234567890abcdef0_18 (gp3, example-b-gp3-throughput – co-tenant using most of the instance's EBS bandwidth)
## Gaps
- VolumeIOPSExceededCheck and VolumeThroughputExceededCheck returned no datapoints for the io2 volume. The IOPS cap is inferred from write ops matching the provisioned IOPS exactly, not from that flag.
- No OS-level data (iostat, the application's queue depth settings) or application latency metrics were looked at. The 'application write latency' is taken to be the EBS per-op latency of about 1.33 ms.

I want to see the actual SSM command parameters sent to the instance to understand the real workload pattern — maybe it's a rate-limited fio job — so I'm going to check the SSM command history for the actual fio configuration used.

Two SSM SendCommand calls and an FIS StopExperiment line up with when the workload started. I'll check the workload definition to rule out an app-side rate limit versus volume throttling before trusting the IOPS-cap explanation.

- **16:18:25 UTC:** an SSM command (`31364f9e-466b-4105-8c00-cd246f57ea52`, sent by `Admin/example-session`) started the `example-a` service. It runs `fio --rw=randwrite --bs=8k --iodepth=32 --runtime=21600` against this volume, with no rate limit. It will try to push as many IOPS as it can for 6 hours.
- **16:19:** writes begin. Before that the volume was idle (0 operations from 15:30 to 16:15).
- **16:20 onward:** writes hold at 999.7–1,000.3 per second every minute. VolumeConsumedReadWriteOps is about 300,000 per 5 minutes, VolumeIdleTime is about 0, and writes are 8 KiB each.
- **16:23:04:** the `example-a-io2-queue-length` alarm fires (VolumeQueueLength about 1.33, threshold 1.0).
- Earlier runs on this volume (Nov 23, 08:00–13:00) also flattened at exactly 1,000 IOPS, so it is the same ceiling each time.

## Why the volume and not the other layers
- **Volume IOPS:** fully used. Demand (32 writes in flight, no rate limit) is far above the 1,000 the volume can deliver.
- **Volume throughput:** not a factor. About 7.8 MiB/s is well below what this io2 volume can move.
- **Instance (c6i.xlarge, i-1234567890abcdef0_3):** not throttling. It uses about 1,500 of its 6,000 baseline IOPS. Both exceeded checks stayed at 0, and both EBS burst balances stayed at 99%.
- **Ruled out:** a fault-injection experiment (template `EXT1234567890abcdef_4`, 500 ms I/O latency) was running, but it targets vol-1234567890abcdef0_11, which isn't attached to this instance.

## Your application sees more latency than CloudWatch shows
CloudWatch puts write latency at about 1.33 ms per operation, but that only counts time after the volume accepts a write. fio keeps 32 writes in flight and only 1,000 complete per second, so each write should take about 32 ms end to end (32 ÷ 1,000/s). The rest of the wait happens before the volume's IOPS limit lets the write through, which CloudWatch doesn't count. That ~32 ms is calculated, not measured (see the last section).

## What to change
1. **Raise the volume's provisioned IOPS** (ModifyVolume). The change applies while the volume stays online. At 10 GiB, io2 allows up to 10,000 IOPS; going higher means growing the volume. After a change, you have to wait 6 hours before modifying the same volume again.
2. **Watch the instance's shared EBS bandwidth when picking the new number.** The instance is already at about 139 of its 156.25 MB/s baseline. Almost all of that is the gp3 volume vol-1234567890abcdef0_18, where the `example-b` job reads about 131 MB/s, that volume's own throughput limit. Each extra 1,000 IOPS on the io2 adds about 8.2 MB/s:
   - **Up to about 3,000 IOPS** fits within the instance baseline.
   - **Above that,** the instance runs on burst credits. Once they run out, the instance becomes the new bottleneck.
3. **If you need more than about 3,000 IOPS,** do one of these as well:
   - move to a larger instance (for example c6i.2xlarge or bigger);
   - throttle or reschedule the gp3 read job;
   - rate-limit the write job (`--rate_iops`).

## What I couldn't check
- **Latency inside the instance:** there's no CloudWatch agent on it and I can't run commands there, so the ~32 ms figure is calculated, not measured.
- **IOPS-exceeded checks:** the volume-level IOPS- and throughput-exceeded metrics exist but returned no data. The cap is inferred from the write rate matching the provisioned 1,000 IOPS exactly.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}

## Results
I'm proposing to raise the provisioned IOPS on io2 volume `vol-0123456789abcdef0` from 1,000 to 3,000, an online change. I did not execute anything. This plan is for you to run. The final version passed the safe-deployment policy check on the third try; the first two were rejected until the plan saved the current volume settings first and checked the result afterwards.

**What I checked before planning (account 012345678901_1, us-east-1):**
- **Volume:** `vol-0123456789abcdef0` (`example-a-io2`) matches the findings: io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000, attached to `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` as `/dev/sdf`.
- **No past changes:** the volume has never been modified (the modification lookup returns `InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound`), so the 6-hour wait between changes doesn't block you now.
- **Co-tenant:** gp3 `vol-1234567890abcdef0_18` is at 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s. The instance (c6i.xlarge, running) also has the root volume `vol-1234567890abcdef0_19` and a fourth data volume, `vol-1234567890abcdef0_15` on `/dev/sdi`.

**Why 3,000 and not 10,000:**
- **The volume limit is what's binding.** An unthrottled iodepth-32 random-write job keeps 32 writes outstanding, so at 1,000 IOPS the application sees about 32 ms per write.
- **Expected gain:** at 3,000 IOPS that should drop to about 10.7 ms. This is an estimate from the queue depth, not a measurement.
- **Why not go higher:** at 3,000 IOPS × 8 KiB, the io2 adds about 24.6 MB/s on top of the co-tenant's ~131 MB/s. That totals about 155.6 MB/s, right at the instance's 156.25 MB/s baseline. Higher IOPS would start using up the instance's burst balance and make the instance the next limit.
- **The alarm may not clear on its own.** fio has no rate limit, so it will push against whatever limit it meets. `VolumeQueueLength` might stay near or above 1.0. The rate limit in step 7 is how to clear it for certain.

## Execution plan

**Prepare**

1. Save the current settings as the rollback baseline:
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json
   ```
   Confirm the file shows io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000.

**Check before applying**

2. Make sure no change is in progress and you're not inside the 6-hour wait:
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   ```
   You want `NotFound`, or a completed change older than 6 hours.
3. Confirm the instance has spare EBS throughput:
   ```
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name EBSByteBalance% --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Minimum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-30 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ) --region us-east-1
   ```
   You want it near 99%. If it is falling, stop and use step 7 instead.

**Apply**

4. Raise the IOPS:
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1
   ```
   - This happens online, with no detach or downtime.
   - Cost goes up: you pay for 2,000 more provisioned IOPS each month.
   - It starts a 6-hour window in which this volume can't be changed again, including undoing this change. Pick the target with that in mind.

**Check afterwards**

5. Confirm the change took:
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   ```
   Check every 1–2 minutes until the state is `optimizing` or `completed` and TargetIops=3000. Size and type should match the saved file.
6. Confirm things got better and nothing new is limiting:
   ```
   aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names example-a-io2-queue-length --region us-east-1
   ```
   - `VolumeWriteOps` should rise to about 900,000 per 5 minutes (about 3,000/s).
   - On `i-1234567890abcdef0_3`, `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` should stay 0, and `EBSByteBalance%` should stay near 99% and not drain.
   - If the byte balance starts to fall, cap the io2 workload (step 7) or slow the co-tenant `example-b` job.

**Optional: cap the workload**

7. Do this if the alarm must clear, or if you want relief without waiting on the volume. Edit the unit with `sudo systemctl edit example-a` on the instance (or via SSM Run Command):
   - Add `--rate_iops=<target>` to the fio `ExecStart` line, for example 900 if you stay at 1,000 IOPS, or about 2,700 at 3,000 IOPS.
   - Or lower `--iodepth`.
   - Then run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart example-a`.
   - To stop it outright: `sudo systemctl stop example-a`.

   This restarts the fio test and it stops pushing at full speed. Confirm with whoever owns the test (the run was started by `assumed-role/Admin/example-session`).

**Rollback**

8. Restore the original IOPS:
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000 --region us-east-1
   ```
   You can only do this once 6 hours have passed since step 4. Until then, stop or rate-limit `example-a` (step 7).

## Permanent fix (code change)

If this volume is defined in infrastructure code, set its provisioned IOPS from the workload's real need so the code doesn't undo the manual change. No repository was identified, so I can't name one.
- **IOPS setting:** io2 `vol-0123456789abcdef0` should have Iops at or above the workload's real need (3,000 to match this plan). Applying the code should not change the volume back to 1,000.
- **Capped benchmarks:** fio units like `example-a` should carry `--rate_iops` (or a bounded iodepth) matched to the volume's IOPS.
- **Instance size:** if the io2 needs well over ~3,000 IOPS while `example-b` keeps reading at full speed, use a larger instance, for example c6i.2xlarge or bigger. Combined io2 and co-tenant throughput should stay under the instance's EBS baseline, so `EBSByteBalance%` doesn't keep draining.

**Gaps:**
- **No pipeline check:** I didn't check for a deployment pipeline. The trigger was a manual SSM command, not a deployment, so the plan uses manual CLI steps.
- **`EbsOptimized` flag:** the instance reports `EbsOptimized=false`. c6i instances are EBS-optimized by default, so I don't expect this to matter. I relied on the investigation's instance EBS limits rather than checking this myself.

# Investigation Summary

## Symptoms

### High VolumeQueueLength on example-a-io2
**Description:** CloudWatch alarm example-a-io2-queue-length (AWS/EBS VolumeQueueLength, Average, 60s, threshold 1.0) moved to ALARM at 2026-11-23 16:23:04 UTC. Three consecutive datapoints of about 1.333 (16:20–16:22). The volume is vol-0123456789abcdef0, io2, 10 GiB, 1000 provisioned IOPS, attached as /dev/sdf to i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (example-perf) in us-east-1a, account 012345678901_1.
**Time:** 2026-11-23T16:20:00Z

## Findings

### Cause: Write workload saturating the io2 volume's 1000 provisioned IOPS
**Description:** A fio randwrite job (8 KiB, iodepth 32, 6 h runtime) was started via SSM at 16:18:25 against io2 vol-0123456789abcdef0. It drives the volume at exactly its provisioned 1,000 IOPS, so writes queue (queue length ~1.33, latency ~1.33 ms). Instance EBS limits are not exceeded.
**Cascades to:** symptom-io2-queue-length

#### Supporting Observations
- **io2 write IOPS pinned at provisioned 1000:** From 16:20 UTC, write IOPS on vol-0123456789abcdef0 have held at about 1000/s, exactly the provisioned 1000 IOPS. Reads are about 0. The workload is 8 KiB writes at about 7.8 MiB/s. Average write latency is about 1.33 ms, and VolumeIdleTime dropped to about 0. Queue length 1.33 ≈ 1000 IOPS × 1.33 ms, which fits a volume running at its IOPS ceiling. Before 16:15 the volume was idle. VolumeIOPSExceededCheck returned no datapoints.
- **Instance-level EBS limits not exceeded:** i-1234567890abcdef0_3 (c6i.xlarge) has a baseline of 6000 IOPS and 156.25 MB/s. Combined EBS traffic was about 1501 IOPS and 139 MB/s, most of it 131 MB/s of reads on the gp3 volume. EBSIOBalance% and EBSByteBalance% held at 99%. InstanceEBSIOPSExceededCheck and InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck stayed at 0. CPU is about 1.2%. Throughput is close to the baseline but under it, so the instance does not look like the bottleneck.

#### Gaps
- **No guest-OS (CWAgent) metrics on the host:** The host has no CloudWatch agent and commands can't be run on it, so latency inside the instance was not measured. End-to-end write latency of about 32 ms (32 in flight ÷ 1,000/s) is calculated, not measured. CloudWatch shows only about 1.33 ms per write because it counts only time after the volume accepts the write.
- **VolumeIOPSExceededCheck returned no data:** The volume-level IOPS- and throughput-exceeded check metrics exist for vol-0123456789abcdef0 but returned no datapoints. The IOPS cap is inferred from the write rate matching the provisioned 1,000 IOPS exactly.

# Mitigation Summary

## Action
Raise provisioned IOPS on io2 vol-0123456789abcdef0 from 1,000 to 3,000 (online ModifyVolume)

## Reasoning
The unthrottled iodepth-32 fio write job is capped by the volume's 1,000 provisioned IOPS, giving an estimated ~32 ms per write. 3,000 IOPS should cut that to about 10.7 ms (estimated). At 3,000 × 8 KiB the io2 adds ~24.6 MB/s to the gp3 co-tenant's ~131 MB/s, about 155.6 MB/s in total, right at the c6i.xlarge's 156.25 MB/s EBS baseline. Going higher would drain burst balance and make the instance the next limit. Because fio is not rate-limited, the queue alarm may not clear on its own; capping the workload is the sure way to clear it. The plan passed the safe-deployment policy check; nothing has been executed.

## Execution Plan

### Step 1: Prepare

#### 1.1 Record the current volume settings
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json
```
**Purpose:** Record the current volume settings. Confirm the file shows io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000.

### Step 2: Pre Validate

#### 2.1 Confirm no modification is in progress or inside the 6-hour cooldown
**Type:** command
```
aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Confirm no modification is in progress or inside the 6-hour cooldown. Expect NotFound, or a completed change older than 6 hours.

#### 2.2 Confirm the instance has spare EBS throughput
**Type:** command
```
aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name EBSByteBalance% --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Minimum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-30 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ) --region us-east-1
```
**Purpose:** Confirm the instance has spare EBS throughput. Expect about 99%; if it is falling, cap the workload instead.

### Step 3: Apply

{"id": "fcf0c096-51ff-4dc6-b87b-87b3e43b8fae", "role": "assistant", "content": [{"text": "I'm proposing to raise the provisioned IOPS on io2 volume `vol-0123456789abcdef0` from 1,000 to 3,000, an online change. I did not execute anything. This plan is for you to run. The final version passed the safe-deployment policy check on the third try; the first two were rejected until the plan saved the current volume settings first and checked the result afterwards.

**What I checked before planning (account 012345678901_1, us-east-1):**
- **Volume:** `vol-0123456789abcdef0` (`example-a-io2`) matches the findings: io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000, attached to `i-1234567890abcdef0_3` as `/dev/sdf`.
- **No past changes:** the volume has never been modified (the modification lookup returns `InvalidVolumeModification.NotFound`), so the 6-hour wait between changes doesn't block you now.
- **Co-tenant:** gp3 `vol-1234567890abcdef0_18` is at 3,000 IOPS and 125 MiB/s. The instance (c6i.xlarge, running) also has the root volume `vol-1234567890abcdef0_19` and a fourth data volume, `vol-1234567890abcdef0_15` on `/dev/sdi`.

**Why 3,000 and not 10,000:**
- **The volume limit is what's binding.** An unthrottled iodepth-32 random-write job keeps 32 writes outstanding, so at 1,000 IOPS the application sees about 32 ms per write.
- **Expected gain:** at 3,000 IOPS that should drop to about 10.7 ms. This is an estimate from the queue depth, not a measurement.
- **Why not go higher:** at 3,000 IOPS × 8 KiB, the io2 adds about 24.6 MB/s on top of the co-tenant's ~131 MB/s. That totals about 155.6 MB/s, right at the instance's 156.25 MB/s baseline. Higher IOPS would start using up the instance's burst balance and make the instance the next limit.
- **The alarm may not clear on its own.** fio has no rate limit, so it will push against whatever limit it meets. `VolumeQueueLength` might stay near or above 1.0. The rate limit in step 7 is how to clear it for certain.

## Execution plan

**Prepare**

1. Save the current settings as the rollback baseline:
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1 > vol-0123456789abcdef0-baseline.json
   ```
   Confirm the file shows io2, 10 GiB, Iops=1000.

**Check before applying**

2. Make sure no change is in progress and you're not inside the 6-hour wait:
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   ```
   You want `NotFound`, or a completed change older than 6 hours.
3. Confirm the instance has spare EBS throughput:
   ```
   aws cloudwatch get-metric-statistics --namespace AWS/EC2 --metric-name EBSByteBalance% --dimensions Name=InstanceId,Value=i-1234567890abcdef0_3 --statistics Minimum --period 60 --start-time $(date -u -d '-30 min' +%FT%TZ) --end-time $(date -u +%FT%TZ) --region us-east-1
   ```
   You want it near 99%. If it is falling, stop and use step 7 instead.

**Apply**

4. Raise the IOPS:
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 3000 --region us-east-1
   ```
   - This happens online, with no detach or downtime.
   - Cost goes up: you pay for 2,000 more provisioned IOPS each month.
   - It starts a 6-hour window in which this volume can't be changed again, including undoing this change. Pick the target with that in mind.

**Check afterwards**

5. Confirm the change took:
   ```
   aws ec2 describe-volumes-modifications --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   aws ec2 describe-volumes --volume-ids vol-0123456789abcdef0 --region us-east-1
   ```
   Check every 1–2 minutes until the state is `optimizing` or `completed` and TargetIops=3000. Size and type should match the saved file.
6. Confirm things got better and nothing new is limiting:
   ```
   aws cloudwatch describe-alarms --alarm-names example-a-io2-queue-length --region us-east-1
   ```
   - `VolumeWriteOps` should rise to about 900,000 per 5 minutes (about 3,000/s).
   - On `i-1234567890abcdef0_3`, `InstanceEBSThroughputExceededCheck` should stay 0, and `EBSByteBalance%` should stay near 99% and not drain.
   - If the byte balance starts to fall, cap the io2 workload (step 7) or slow the co-tenant `example-b` job.

**Optional: cap the workload**

7. Do this if the alarm must clear, or if you want relief without waiting on the volume. Edit the unit with `sudo systemctl edit example-a` on the instance (or via SSM Run Command):
   - Add `--rate_iops=<target>` to the fio `ExecStart` line, for example 900 if you stay at 1,000 IOPS, or about 2,700 at 3,000 IOPS.
   - Or lower `--iodepth`.
   - Then run `sudo systemctl daemon-reload && sudo systemctl restart example-a`.
   - To stop it outright: `sudo systemctl stop example-a`.

   This restarts the fio test and it stops pushing at full speed. Confirm with whoever owns the test (the run was started by `assumed-role/Admin/example-session`).

**Rollback**

8. Restore the original IOPS:
   ```
   aws ec2 modify-volume --volume-id vol-0123456789abcdef0 --iops 1000 --region us-east-1
   ```
   You can only do this once 6 hours have passed since step 4. Until then, stop or rate-limit `example-a` (step 7).

## Permanent fix (code change)

If this volume is defined in infrastructure code, set its provisioned IOPS from the workload's real need so the code doesn't undo the manual change. No repository was identified, so I can't name one.
- **IOPS setting:** io2 `vol-0123456789abcdef0` should have Iops at or above the workload's real need (3,000 to match this plan). Applying the code should not change the volume back to 1,000.
- **Capped benchmarks:** fio units like `example-a` should carry `--rate_iops` (or a bounded iodepth) matched to the volume's IOPS.
- **Instance size:** if the io2 needs well over ~3,000 IOPS while `example-b` keeps reading at full speed, use a larger instance, for example c6i.2xlarge or bigger. Combined io2 and co-tenant throughput should stay under the instance's EBS baseline, so `EBSByteBalance%` doesn't keep draining.

**Gaps:**
- **No pipeline check:** I didn't check for a deployment pipeline. The trigger was a manual SSM command, not a deployment, so the plan uses manual CLI steps.
- **`EbsOptimized` flag:** the instance reports `EbsOptimized=false`. c6i instances are EBS-optimized by default, so I don't expect this to matter. I relied on the investigation's instance EBS limits rather than checking this myself.", "type": "text"}], "user_reference": null}
